questions.question: Roots spread out under the soil and hold a plant firmly in place. What other job do a plant's roots do?
questions.context: Roots soak up water and minerals from the soil, mostly through fine root hairs that give them a far bigger surface. Minerals are not food: a plant makes its food in its leaves, and its flowers, with their bright petals that draw in insects, make the seeds.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 4-LS1-1 and 5-LS1-1 (map line G5.L3) teach the jobs of a plant's parts, and roots taking in water and minerals is the first of them.

questions.question: A white carnation stands in a jar of water coloured with blue dye. A day later, its petals are streaked with blue. What are the tiny tubes that carried the blue water up the stem called?
questions.context: Xylem tubes carry water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves and flowers, and the dye rides up with the water. Phloem tubes carry the sugar made in the leaves to the rest of the plant, stomata are tiny pores in the leaves, and chlorophyll is the green colouring that catches light.
questions.grade_note: The map line G5.L3 (Core Knowledge Grade 5, Plant Structures and Processes) names xylem as the stem's water tubes, and the dyed white flower is a standard classroom test of it.

questions.question: The underside of a leaf is dotted with tiny pores called stomata. Two small cells around each pore open and close it, like a pair of doors. What do the stomata let in and out of the leaf?
questions.context: Carbon dioxide from the air comes in through the stomata, and oxygen and water vapour go out; in dry weather the two cells close the pores to save water. Sunlight shines straight through the leaf's clear skin, minerals come up from the roots in the xylem, and sugar travels in the phloem.
questions.grade_note: The map line G5.L3 (NGSS 5-LS1-1; Core Knowledge Grade 5) teaches that tiny leaf pores, the stomata, let gases in and out.

questions.question: A bumblebee drinks nectar from a flower, and fine dust from the flower clings to its furry body. Some of it rubs off on the next flower of that kind, which can then make seeds. What is this carrying of dust between flowers called?
questions.context: The dust is pollen, made by the flower's stamens, and pollination is its journey to another flower of the same kind so that seeds can form. Bees, butterflies, birds, bats and the wind all carry pollen; seed dispersal comes later, when the finished seeds are spread, and germination is a seed sprouting.
questions.grade_note: Grades 3-5 plant lessons (US Botanic Garden; Oak National Academy Year 5) name pollination as a stage in a flowering plant's life, after NGSS 2-LS2-2 brings it in early.

questions.question: An acorn grows from one of an oak tree's tiny flowers, and inside its hard shell lies a seed. To a scientist, what kind of plant part is an acorn?
questions.context: To a scientist, a fruit is the part that grows from a flower and holds and protects its seeds, so acorns and maple helicopters are fruits, though neither is sweet. A pine cone holds seeds too, but pines have no flowers, so a cone is not a fruit.
questions.grade_note: Grades 3-5 plant lessons (US Botanic Garden) teach that a flower grows into the fruit that holds and protects its seeds, which makes an acorn a fruit.

questions.question: Some seeds ride the wind, some hitch a ride on animals, and some float away on water. Which of these drifts across the sea to new shores?
questions.context: A coconut's husk is full of air pockets, so it floats, and ocean currents can carry it to far shores while the seed inside stays alive for months. Dandelion seeds ride the wind on fluffy parachutes, maple helicopters spin on the wind, and burrs hook onto passing animals' fur.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade plant life-cycle lessons (Oak National Academy Year 5) teach seed dispersal, and wind, water and animals are the three ways they name for it.

questions.question: A bean seed lies on a damp paper towel in a clear jar. After a few days its skin splits, and the young plant inside starts to grow out. Which part of the young plant comes out first?
questions.context: The young root comes out first and grows down, ready to hold the seedling in place and take in water. Only after that does the shoot, the young stem with its first leaves, push up toward the light.
questions.grade_note: Germination opens the flowering-plant life cycle in 5th-grade units (Oak National Academy Year 5), and seeds sprouting on a damp towel or cotton pad are a common classroom test (US Botanic Garden grades 3-5).

questions.question: A bean seed soaked overnight slips out of its thin skin and splits into two thick halves, with a tiny plant tucked between them. What do the two thick halves do for the tiny plant?
questions.answer: Feed it as it starts to grow
choices: Feed it as it starts to grow
Hold air for it to breathe
Take in water from the soil
questions.context: The two halves are the bean's seed leaves, packed with food that the parent plant stored there, and they feed the young plant until it can make its own food in the light. The seed draws in water and air from around it, its thin skin (the seed coat) protects it, and the root grows from the tiny plant itself.
questions.grade_note: Grades 3-5 seed lessons (US Botanic Garden; NSTA's Needs of Seeds probe) teach that a seed holds a young plant, a store of food made by the parent, and a protective coat.

questions.question: Many wild plants wrap their seeds in bright, sweet berries. How do the berries help the plant?
questions.answer: Animals eat them and spread the seeds
choices: Animals eat them and spread the seeds
Bees feed on them and carry their pollen
They hold water for the dry summer
They keep the seeds warm in winter
questions.context: Birds and other animals eat the sweet flesh, and the seeds pass through them unharmed and drop out in their droppings, often far from the parent plant. Pollen comes from flowers, and a berry grows only after its flower has been pollinated.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 2-LS2-2 introduces animals spreading seeds, and 5th-grade life-cycle units (Oak National Academy Year 5) teach seed dispersal and warn that pupils mix it up with pollination.
